summary: Addresses the OSPF demand circuit extension, which suppresses Hello packets to reduce overhead. It describes a way to detect inactive neighbors over such circuits so the circuit can go down when no interesting traffic remains.

eli5.summary: If two friends stop talking, they should notice and hang up the call so they do not pay for silence. This document helps routers notice.

questions: what is an ospf demand circuit
how does ospf detect inactive neighbors on demand circuits
subtitle: How OSPF routers can check that a neighbor across a demand circuit is still running OSPF, without keeping the link busy.

tldr.problem: On OSPF demand circuits Hello packets are suppressed so the link can go down when idle, which makes it impossible to notice that the neighbor's OSPF has failed.
tldr.mechanism: Neighbor probing re-floods an LSA the neighbor should already have and waits for an acknowledgement. If none comes after the retransmission limit, the adjacency is brought down.
tldr.outcome: It is backward-compatible with standard OSPF and disabled by default, but adds traffic whenever the link is up. The RFC updates RFC 1793.

today: RFC 3883 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1793. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem: Silent Failures
sections.content:
OSPF is a link-state routing protocol. RFC 1793 optimizes it for demand circuits to minimize overhead traffic. One part of that is Hello suppression, which lets the circuit go down when no interesting traffic is flowing.

The side effect is that a router can no longer tell that its neighbor has stopped running OSPF. The RFC gives two example causes: the OSPF process might have died on the neighbor, or oversubscription (Section 7 of RFC 1793) may cause continuous drops of application data at the link level. If other routers cannot report what they know through flooding, the local router and the routers behind it may keep forwarding traffic to a neighbor that cannot route it.
sections.eli5: Normally friends keep saying hello to check they are still there. On a pay-per-minute call they stop saying hello to save money, so nobody notices if one friend has wandered off.

sections.title: Neighbor Probing in Outline
sections.content:
The solution uses link state update packets to find out whether OSPF is working on the remote neighbor. Either router on a demand circuit may test the other at any time. It applies to point-to-point links, virtual links and point-to-multipoint interfaces. Broadcast and NBMA networks are not considered, since Hello suppression is not used there.

After the routers have synchronized their link state databases, the circuit may be torn down when idle and brought up again when application traffic starts. If ospfIfDemandNbrProbe is enabled, the routers SHOULD probe each other. While the link is up they may also probe periodically, every ospfIfDemandNbrProbeInterval.

Probing is not interesting traffic and must not keep the circuit up. If a link is oversubscribed, probing should be restricted to neighbors that are actually reachable at that moment, so a temporarily unreachable neighbor is not wrongly declared down. How to check this is left to the implementation.
sections.eli5: Either router can ask the other, now and then, whether it is still there. Asking must not count as a real conversation, or the call would never be allowed to end.

sections.title: How a Probe Works
sections.content:
To verify a neighbor, a router floods to it any LSA that would normally be sent during the initial database synchronization. For example, it can flood its own router-LSA without originating a new version, or the neighbor's own router-LSA. A live, OSPF-capable neighbor answers with a link state acknowledgement or a link state update, which counts as an implied acknowledgement, and the LSA leaves the retransmission list.

If no acknowledgement arrives within a predefined time, the probing router treats this as evidence that the neighbor is unreachable and should bring the adjacency down. The number of retransmissions of a probe LSA should be limited to ospfIfDemandNbrProbeRetxLimit.

The probe LSA has the same contents as the one the neighbor already holds, so it normally causes no extra flooding. Because LSA refreshes are not flooded over demand circuits, it may carry a higher sequence number, in which case the first probe is flooded further by the neighbor. Later probes do not cause more flooding until the sequence number increases. Implementations should also make sure probe packets do not prevent the circuit from being torn down.
sections.eli5: A router repeats something it already told its neighbor and waits for a thumbs-up. If the thumbs-up never comes after several tries, it decides the neighbor is gone.

sections.title: Configurable Parameters
sections.content:
Appendix A defines three additional configuration parameters for OSPF interfaces.

  • ospfIfDemandNbrProbe says whether neighbor probing is enabled. It is disabled by default.
  • ospfIfDemandNbrProbeRetxLimit is the number of consecutive LSA retransmissions before the neighbor is deemed inactive and the adjacency is brought down. The sample value is 10.
  • ospfIfDemandNbrProbeInterval sets how often the neighbor is probed. The sample value is 2 minutes.
sections.eli5: There are three dials: whether to check at all (off to begin with), how many unanswered tries before giving up, and how often to check.

sections.title: Compatibility and Special Links
sections.content:
The method is completely compatible with standard OSPF implementations, because it relies on behavior that OSPF implementations must follow anyway to keep their databases synchronized. A neighbor needs no new software to answer a probe.

Virtual links can be treated like point-to-point links, so the same techniques apply. A point-to-multipoint interface running as a demand circuit (Section 3.5 of RFC 1793) can be treated as individual point-to-point links.
sections.eli5: The check uses a question every router already knows how to answer, so old routers do not have to learn anything new.

sections.title: Costs and Security
sections.content:
Besides the lost functionality noted in Section 6 of RFC 1793, probing adds overhead in link state updates and acknowledgements whenever the link is up, which raises the overall cost of the link.

The Security Considerations section is a single statement: the mechanism does not modify the security aspects of the OSPF routing protocol.
sections.eli5: Checking costs a little bit of talking, so the call costs slightly more. It does not change how safe OSPF is.
